decisions.title: Structured sources require one object-shaped document
decisions.specification: RFC 8259 The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
decisions.issue: JSON permits any serialized value and YAML permits streams containing arbitrary root nodes, while configuration loading requires one mergeable document shape.
interpretations: Accept every specification-valid root and define format-specific merge rules.
Require one object, mapping, or root table and reject additional documents or root values.
decisions.peer_behavior: General-purpose JSON and YAML decoders commonly accept scalar, sequence, and multi-document inputs; TOML always exposes a root table.
decisions.selected_behavior: Each structured source produces exactly one map[string]any root. JSON scalars, arrays, null, and trailing roots fail; YAML requires exactly one mapping document; TOML uses its root table.
decisions.rationale: A single object-shaped document gives merge and decode one deterministic key-addressable input without inventing scalar or multi-document precedence.
decisions.security_consequences: Rejecting additional roots prevents hidden trailing configuration and avoids partial selection from multi-document streams.
decisions.resource_consequences: Only one bounded document is converted and retained.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: Previously rejected non-object roots remain errors across structured sources.
decisions.wire_consequences: Accepted source bytes are not rewritten; the restriction applies to the loaded configuration tree.
decisions.upstream_status: No upstream issue exists because the root restriction is application policy.
decisions.reconsider_when: The merge model gains an explicit scalar, sequence, or multi-document composition contract.

decisions.title: Duplicate member definitions fail closed
decisions.specification: RFC 8259 The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
decisions.issue: JSON only recommends unique object names and peer decoders disagree on first-wins, last-wins, all-values, or rejection behavior; YAML and TOML require unique mapping or key definitions.
interpretations: Keep the first definition.
Keep the last definition.
Expose every duplicate.
Reject the document before publishing a tree.
decisions.peer_behavior: encoding/json keeps the last duplicate object value, while YAML and TOML parsers vary in diagnostics and rejection timing.
decisions.selected_behavior: JSON, YAML, and TOML reject duplicate definitions. JSON and YAML report a safe key path, YAML also reports location, and no partial tree is published.
decisions.rationale: Failing closed follows JSON's interoperability recommendation and preserves YAML and TOML uniqueness instead of silently selecting authority by parser order.
decisions.security_consequences: An attacker cannot smuggle a shadow value that different readers interpret differently.
decisions.resource_consequences: Duplicate detection uses the same bounded key accounting as normal conversion.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: Duplicate configuration remains invalid rather than acquiring first-wins or last-wins semantics.
decisions.wire_consequences: No ambiguous document produces a normalized tree.
decisions.upstream_status: RFC 8259 documents the peer divergence; no package-specific upstream issue exists.
decisions.reconsider_when: A versioned compatibility mode explicitly exposes a different duplicate-member policy.

decisions.title: Shared numeric values use bounded Go scalar types
decisions.specification: RFC 8259 The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
decisions.issue: The formats define numeric syntax but do not select the Go types, precision, or overflow behavior of one cross-format configuration tree.
interpretations: Convert every number to float64.
Preserve parser-specific numeric types.
Use arbitrary-precision values.
Normalize integers to int64 then uint64 and finite fractional values to float64.
decisions.peer_behavior: encoding/json defaults to float64 unless UseNumber is enabled; YAML and TOML decoders expose source-specific numeric types.
decisions.selected_behavior: Signed integers normalize to int64, larger non-negative integers through math.MaxUint64 normalize to uint64, finite fractional and exponent values normalize to float64, and values outside the supported domain fail.
decisions.rationale: The bounded scalar set preserves common integer precision, supports typed decoding, and keeps equivalent finite documents equal across formats.
decisions.security_consequences: Overflow and non-finite conversion errors fail without including the sensitive numeric token.
decisions.resource_consequences: Numeric conversion has fixed memory and does not allocate arbitrary-precision values.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: The normalized Go scalar types and overflow boundaries remain part of the source contract.
decisions.wire_consequences: Numeric source syntax is consumed into a canonical tree and is not serialized back to the original format.
decisions.upstream_status: No upstream issue exists because Go scalar selection is package-owned.
decisions.reconsider_when: The public tree model adopts an explicit arbitrary-precision numeric value type.

decisions.title: Non-finite numbers remain source-language specific
decisions.issue: JSON forbids Infinity and NaN, YAML core resolution can produce non-finite floats, and TOML 1.0.0 explicitly defines inf and nan while the common tree uses float64.
interpretations: Reject non-finite values in every format.
Accept every parser's non-finite values.
Preserve TOML's normative values while keeping JSON and the defensive YAML profile finite-only.
decisions.peer_behavior: TOML decoders normally expose inf and nan as floating-point values; JSON parsers reject them and YAML parsers vary by schema and safety profile.
decisions.selected_behavior: JSON rejects non-finite syntax, YAML rejects resolved infinity and NaN scalars, and TOML preserves inf, -inf, and nan as float64 values.
decisions.rationale: The policy preserves valid TOML 1.0.0 data without broadening JSON grammar or the deliberately finite YAML configuration profile.
decisions.security_consequences: Callers decoding TOML floating-point values must handle non-finite values explicitly; other formats cannot introduce them.
decisions.resource_consequences: Non-finite TOML values use ordinary float64 storage.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: TOML callers retain accepted non-finite values while JSON and YAML remain finite-only.
decisions.wire_consequences: The distinction is source-format specific and visible only in the normalized Go tree.
decisions.upstream_status: No upstream issue exists; the package intentionally chooses a narrower YAML profile and preserves TOML 1.0.0 values.
decisions.reconsider_when: The canonical tree adopts a format-independent finite-number restriction.

decisions.title: YAML graph and application tag features are disabled
decisions.issue: YAML supports aliases, anchors, application tags, complex keys, and graph structures that do not map safely or unambiguously into the package's JSON-shaped configuration tree.
interpretations: Expose the complete YAML representation graph.
Expand aliases and merge keys.
Allow registered application tags.
Accept only core scalar, sequence, and string-keyed mapping nodes without aliases.
decisions.peer_behavior: General-purpose YAML loaders commonly expand aliases and may resolve application tags or merge keys; safety-focused configuration loaders often disable them.
decisions.selected_behavior: YAML accepts core scalar, sequence, and mapping nodes with string keys, but rejects aliases, merge keys, custom tags, non-string keys, tagged collections, and multiple documents.
decisions.rationale: The bounded tree model has no identity, executable tag, or complex-key semantics, so accepting those features would create hidden expansion and format-only behavior.
decisions.security_consequences: Disabling aliases and application tags prevents expansion attacks, object construction, and merge-key shadowing.
decisions.resource_consequences: Conversion work is bounded by explicit depth and key limits without alias expansion.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: Documents using advanced YAML graph or tag features remain rejected and must be rewritten as explicit core values.
decisions.wire_consequences: Accepted YAML is normalized to an acyclic map and slice tree.
decisions.upstream_status: The YAML specification permits application-specific availability decisions; no package-specific upstream issue exists.
decisions.reconsider_when: A separate opt-in YAML graph API defines identity, expansion, tag registration, and resource ownership.

decisions.title: YAML timestamps normalize to inert strings
decisions.issue: YAML tag resolution and parser compatibility behavior can surface timestamp-shaped scalars as native time values even though the common configuration tree has no timezone or calendar value type.
interpretations: Expose parser-native time.Time values.
Reject timestamp-resolved scalars.
Normalize the resolved lexical value to a string.
decisions.peer_behavior: YAML libraries differ by schema and compatibility mode on whether timestamp-shaped plain scalars become strings or native date-time values.
decisions.selected_behavior: A YAML scalar resolved as a timestamp is returned as its lexical string value without timezone conversion or clock interpretation.
decisions.rationale: Strings preserve inert configuration data and align timestamp-shaped values with JSON while avoiding implicit calendar semantics.
decisions.security_consequences: Loading configuration cannot trigger timezone lookup or time-based side effects.
decisions.resource_consequences: Timestamp normalization allocates only the bounded scalar string.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: YAML timestamp-shaped values remain strings in Document.Tree.
decisions.wire_consequences: The lexical timestamp is preserved as a string rather than converted to a canonical time instant.
decisions.upstream_status: go.yaml.in/yaml v4 documents preserved YAML 1.1 compatibility behavior; no package-specific upstream issue exists.
decisions.reconsider_when: The public tree introduces an explicit date-time value with documented timezone semantics.

decisions.title: TOML date and time values normalize to strings
decisions.section: Offset Date-Time, Local Date-Time, Local Date, and Local Time
decisions.issue: TOML defines four date and time types, but the common configuration tree must choose whether to preserve parser-native time.Time values, distinguish TOML categories, or expose strings.
interpretations: Expose time.Time and parser locations.
Create four package-specific temporal types.
Normalize each TOML category to a stable lexical string.
decisions.peer_behavior: BurntSushi TOML represents all four categories with time.Time plus synthetic locations for local categories.
decisions.selected_behavior: Offset date-time values use RFC3339Nano strings; local date-time, local date, and local time use fixed lexical layouts without adding a timezone.
decisions.rationale: String normalization preserves category meaning, avoids synthetic location leakage, and aligns date-time-shaped values with JSON and YAML configuration.
decisions.security_consequences: Configuration loading performs no timezone lookup or clock-dependent conversion.
decisions.resource_consequences: Normalization uses bounded fixed-layout string formatting.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: All TOML date and time categories remain strings in Document.Tree.
decisions.wire_consequences: Date and time values are normalized to stable strings and are not serialized back to TOML.
decisions.upstream_status: No upstream issue exists because the mapping from TOML temporal values to the package tree is application policy.
decisions.reconsider_when: The public tree introduces explicit local and offset temporal value types.

decisions.title: Equivalent structured documents share one canonical tree
decisions.specification: RFC 8259 The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
decisions.issue: JSON, YAML, and TOML have overlapping but non-identical data models, so parser-native outputs can make precedence and typed decoding depend on the source format.
interpretations: Expose each parser's native value graph.
Normalize only at typed decode time.
Normalize the shared object, array, string, boolean, and finite-number subset before merge and document language-specific gaps.
decisions.peer_behavior: Format-specific libraries expose distinct integer, timestamp, table-array, null, and graph representations.
decisions.selected_behavior: Equivalent objects, arrays of objects, strings, booleans, and finite numbers normalize identically before merge. JSON and YAML null become nil; TOML has no null. Timestamp and TOML date-time values normalize to strings.
decisions.rationale: Pre-merge normalization makes source substitution predictable while preserving explicit differences that the source languages cannot share.
decisions.security_consequences: Format substitution cannot silently activate aliases, tags, or parser-native object types.
decisions.resource_consequences: Normalization copies only bounded trees and does not retain parser graphs.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: Equivalent documents continue to produce deeply equal Document.Tree values across formats.
decisions.wire_consequences: The package defines a canonical in-memory tree, not a canonical serialized wire format.
decisions.upstream_status: No upstream standard defines the package's cross-format tree; this is an application interoperability contract.
decisions.reconsider_when: A new structured source cannot map its shared values without weakening an existing normalized type or invariant.

decisions.title: Structured parsing is bounded and diagnostics are redacted
decisions.specification: RFC 8259 The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
decisions.issue: The format specifications permit implementations to set limits but do not define this library's byte, depth, key, cancellation, diagnostic, or secret-redaction boundaries.
interpretations: Delegate all limits and errors to parser defaults.
Apply only a byte limit.
Enforce common byte, depth, and key limits with cancellation and redact parser details.
decisions.peer_behavior: General-purpose parsers expose detailed syntax errors and format-specific resource behavior; their defaults are not a shared hostile-input contract.
decisions.selected_behavior: Each structured source enforces caller-configurable byte, depth, and key limits, checks cancellation during owned work, publishes no partial tree, and exposes stable errors without source tokens.
decisions.rationale: Configuration may contain secrets and can be attacker-controlled, so bounded work and redacted failure surfaces are package-owned requirements.
decisions.security_consequences: Hostile inputs cannot request unbounded owned traversal or leak source contents through public diagnostics.
decisions.resource_consequences: Default limits are 1 MiB, depth 64, and 100000 keys, with caller-selected positive overrides.
decisions.compatibility_consequences: Inputs beyond configured limits and detailed dependency error messages remain unavailable.
decisions.wire_consequences: Rejected input produces no normalized document.
decisions.upstream_status: RFC 8259 allows implementation limits; YAML and TOML do not define the package's common resource and diagnostic policy.
decisions.reconsider_when: A parser backend changes owned cancellation or traversal boundaries, or the public limit model changes.
